title: Living Abroad No Shield: Court Orders NRI Couple in Germany to Face Dowry Trial
excerpt: A Ghaziabad sessions court dismissed a Germany-based couple's petition to be discharged from a dowry harassment case, ruling they must appear for trial in India.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • A Ghaziabad court ruled NRIs Ankit and Silky Jain must face dowry trial in India.
  • The couple's petition for discharge was dismissed due to lack of legal grounds.
  • The case involves dowry demands during a wedding costing Rs 50–55 lakh in 2019.
  • Living abroad does not exempt NRIs from Indian criminal proceedings under Section 498A.
  • Indian courts consistently uphold that NRIs must face charges regardless of their residence.
Court Ruling on NRI Dowry Case
›Couple must appear for trial in India.
›Charges filed under IPC Sections 498A, 323, 504, 506.
›Initial dismissal of their names from chargesheet due to insufficient evidence.
›Reinstated after evidence presented during trial.
›Trial set for February 25, 2025.
Ghaziabad Sessions Court

The Case

A sessions court in Ghaziabad has dismissed a revision petition filed by Ankit and Silky Jain, an NRI couple living in Germany, who sought discharge from a dowry harassment case in which they are named as co-accused.

The case was filed by Ankit's sister-in-law, Urvarshi, on August 26, 2020. She alleged that after her marriage to Ankit's brother Abhishek on November 9, 2019 — in a wedding costing Rs 50–55 lakh — her in-laws, including Ankit and Silky who had traveled from Germany for the ceremony, pressured her for additional dowry.

The original FIR named five people: the couple, Abhishek, and their parents Sushil Kumar and Archana. Charges were filed under multiple sections of the Indian Penal Code, including Section 498A (matrimonial cruelty), Section 323 (voluntarily causing hurt), and Sections 504 and 506 (criminal intimidation), along with Section 3/4 of the Dowry Prohibition Act.

Dropped, Then Reinstated

Police initially dropped Ankit and Silky's names from the chargesheet, citing insufficient evidence. But after the magistrate's court framed charges against the other accused in October 2022, Urvarshi filed an application under Section 319 of the Criminal Procedure Code — the provision that allows courts to proceed against additional persons who appear guilty based on evidence presented during trial.

Urvarshi alleged the NRI couple had conspired with the investigating officer to have their names removed from the chargesheet. During her examination, she reiterated claims about dowry demands made during the couple's month-long visit for the wedding.

The trial court summoned Ankit and Silky for trial in a February 25, 2025 order. They subsequently filed a criminal revision petition before the sessions court.

The Court's Ruling

In their plea, Ankit and Silky argued they had never lived with Urvarshi except briefly during the wedding period, pointed to contradictions in her FIR, police statement, and court testimony, and called her allegations malicious.

Additional Sessions Judge Neeraj Gautam was unmoved. Citing Supreme Court precedent on the limited scope of revisional jurisdiction, the judge held that the lower court's order showed "no legal error warranting interference."

"The object of the provisions of revision is to set right a patent defect or an error of jurisdiction or law."

— Additional Sessions Judge Neeraj Gautam

The court ruled that a revision petition could only succeed where decisions are "grossly erroneous," findings are "based on no evidence," or "judicial discretion is exercised arbitrarily or perversely." None of those conditions were met.

Implications for NRIs

The ruling carries a clear message for India's overseas diaspora: living abroad provides no automatic shield from Indian criminal proceedings.

Section 498A of the IPC, which addresses cruelty by a husband or his relatives, has long been a contentious provision. Supporters say it is essential for protecting women from dowry-related abuse. Critics, including some NRI advocacy groups, argue it is frequently weaponized to drag distant family members into protracted litigation.

For NRIs, the practical consequences are severe. Court appearances require international travel, and non-compliance with summons can lead to warrants and complications with passport renewal. The couple has been ordered to appear for trial under Section 498A and the Dowry Prohibition Act.

A Broader Pattern

Implications for NRIs in Legal Cases
›Living abroad does not shield from Indian laws.
›Court appearances require international travel.
›Non-compliance can lead to warrants and passport issues.
›Legal advice is crucial for NRIs facing charges.
›Indian citizenship entails legal obligations worldwide.
Legal experts' insights

This is not an isolated case. Indian courts have consistently held that NRIs cannot claim exemption from criminal proceedings simply by virtue of residing abroad. In recent years, several high-profile cases have seen NRI family members summoned back to India to face charges under matrimonial and dowry laws.

Legal experts advise NRIs named in such cases to engage Indian counsel early rather than assume that geographic distance will lead to eventual dismissal. The Jain case is the latest reminder that Indian citizenship and its legal obligations follow you wherever you live.
image_caption: A court gavel in an Indian courtroom. A Ghaziabad sessions court dismissed a revision petition filed by an NRI couple seeking discharge from a dowry harassment case.
nri_angle: The ruling underscores that NRIs living abroad remain subject to Indian criminal proceedings, with significant legal and practical consequences for the diaspora.
